meta.title: The Bottom Set, Where Minor Runs Out First
meta.summary: The same one-fret move as every other set, except down here minor's narrow gap sits at the bottom of the grip, exactly where the neck's room runs out first.

spans.text: One more set, one more fret dropped — and this is the set where that fret costs something. The third still comes down a semitone, same as it has all chapter. What's different on strings 4-5-6 is how little room is left when it does.

Time to be precise about mud, because down here it's easy to overstate the danger. The app's voicing engine rejects two adjacent notes sitting too close together too low: below
it wants at least a major third between them, below
at least two. Every one of C minor's twelve grips passes every one of those rules, exactly as every one of C major's does. None of them are muddy. What is true is how little room is left.

What actually differs, and it's the whole lesson: minor stacks its two gaps in the opposite order from major's. Major's root position goes 4 semitones then 3, bass to third to fifth. Minor goes 3 then 4 — the narrow gap moves down to the bottom of the grip, and the bottom is exactly where the mud rule is strictest.

Chapter 2's floor on this set was G major root position, both gaps sitting exactly on the app's limit. Minor's floor sits two semitones higher, and it isn't a C chord — worth leaving the anchor key for one example, same as chapter 2 did.

When to reach for this set at all, chapter 2 already made the arrangement case — a bass player's register, filling the bottom when you're playing alone — and it applies to minor just as much. What's specific to minor: the
sits a semitone closer to the bass than a major third does, so a low minor triad asks more of the room it's sitting in than the major one at the same pitch.
